--- title: "Discriminative and generative models" description: "A discriminative model learns only the answer; a generative model learns the data well enough to invent new examples. k-nearest neighbours and a pair of bell curves answer the same presence question on the coastal survey, and part company where the data are thin." order: 4 categories: [foundations, supervised, classification] --- {{< new-terms >}} ## A model learns either the answer or the data [Types of learning](types-of-learning.qmd) sorted methods by the data you hold. This page sorts them a second way: by what the model learns. Suppose the question is whether a species is present, given the water temperature. A model can learn one of two things. A **discriminative model** learns the answer directly: the chance that the species is present at each temperature. It draws the boundary between "present" and "absent" and nothing else. Most methods in this course are discriminative, including k-nearest neighbours, decision trees, random forests and neural networks. A **generative model** learns the data themselves. It describes the temperatures where the species was found, and separately the temperatures where it was not. To classify a new station, it asks which of the two descriptions fits that station's temperature better. Because it has learned the data, it can also *generate* new ones: plausible temperatures for a place where the species occurs. The tools that write text or draw pictures are generative models of the same kind, on a vastly larger scale. ::: {.diagram} ![The same data seen by two kinds of model. A discriminative model learns only the boundary between the groups; a generative model learns a description of each group, from which it can draw new examples.](img/discriminative-generative.svg){fig-alt="Two panels showing the same scatter of stations by temperature and depth: blue dots where the species was found, orange triangles where it was not. In the left panel, labelled discriminative, a dashed line separates the two groups. In the right panel, labelled generative, a shaded oval surrounds each group, and a hollow dot inside the blue oval is marked as a new example."} ::: ## Both kinds answer the presence question ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: Both models below answer the presence question for the coastal survey, with temperature as the only input. They learn from the same three quarters of the stations, the training set, and are asked about the same three new stations: a warm one at 12 °C, one at 9 °C and a cold one at 3 °C. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey() split <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75, strata = present) train <- training(split) new_stations <- tibble( station = c("warm", "middle", "cold"), temperature_c = c(12, 9, 3) ) ``` ::: ### k-nearest neighbours learns only the answer k-nearest neighbours, from [Types of learning](types-of-learning.qmd), is the discriminative model. For a new station it finds the 15 training stations with the closest temperatures and reports the share of them that had the species. With a single input there is nothing to put on a common scale, so it needs no recipe. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} discriminative <- nearest_neighbor(neighbors = 15, weight_func = "rectangular") |> set_engine("kknn") |> set_mode("classification") |> fit(present ~ temperature_c, data = train) bind_cols(new_stations, predict(discriminative, new_stations, type = "prob")) |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station | temperature_c| .pred_yes| .pred_no| |:-------|-------------:|---------:|--------:| |warm | 12| 0.8| 0.2| |middle | 9| 1.0| 0.0| |cold | 3| 0.0| 1.0|
::: ::: For each new station it returns one thing: the chance of presence, and its complement. At 9 °C, 15 of the 15 nearest stations had the species, so the chance is 100%; at 12 °C it is 80% and at 3 °C 0%. That is all the model knows. It holds no description of cold or warm water, only the stations themselves. ### A generative model fits one bell curve per group The generative model describes the temperatures at stations with the species by a **Normal distribution**: the familiar bell-shaped curve, centred on the group's mean temperature, with its width set by the group's sd. It does the same for the stations without the species, and records how common each group is. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} generative <- train |> group_by(present) |> summarise(mean = mean(temperature_c), sd = sd(temperature_c), share = n() / nrow(train)) generative |> mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 2))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|present | mean| sd| share| |:-------|----:|----:|-----:| |yes | 8.95| 2.39| 0.78| |no | 8.11| 3.71| 0.22|
::: ::: The two groups have similar mean temperatures, 8.95 °C with the species and 8.11 °C without, but the stations without it spread much more widely (sd 3.71 °C against 2.39 °C): the species is missing mainly from the coldest and the warmest water. The height of a bell curve at a given temperature is its **density**: high where that temperature is common in the group, low where it is rare. To classify a new station, **Bayes' rule** weighs the two groups: the density of each group's bell curve at the station's temperature, times how common that group is. The chance of presence is the "present" group's share of the total. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p_present_generative <- function(temperature) { yes <- filter(generative, present == "yes") no <- filter(generative, present == "no") fit_yes <- yes$share * dnorm(temperature, yes$mean, yes$sd) fit_no <- no$share * dnorm(temperature, no$mean, no$sd) fit_yes / (fit_yes + fit_no) } new_stations |> mutate(.pred_yes = round(p_present_generative(temperature_c), 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|station | temperature_c| .pred_yes| |:-------|-------------:|---------:| |warm | 12| 0.80| |middle | 9| 0.85| |cold | 3| 0.39|
::: ::: Because it holds a description of the data, it can also generate new data. Here are five plausible temperatures for stations where the species lives, drawn from its bell curve: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} with(yes_group, round(rnorm(5, mean, sd), 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] 7.5 6.1 9.2 6.7 9.1 ``` ::: ::: ## The two part company where the data are thin @fig-two-models puts the two side by side. The left panel is the generative model's view: the data of each group, and the bell curve it fitted. The right panel shows the answer both models give, the chance of presence at every temperature. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} curves <- tibble(temperature_c = seq(2, 16, by = 0.1)) |> mutate( `k-nearest neighbours` = predict(discriminative, pick(temperature_c), type = "prob")$.pred_yes, `Bell curves` = p_present_generative(temperature_c) ) |> pivot_longer(-temperature_c, names_to = "model", values_to = "p") bell <- generative |> reframe(temperature_c = seq(0, 18, by = 0.1), density = dnorm(temperature_c, mean, sd), .by = present) |> mutate(group = if_else(present == "yes", "Species found", "Species not found")) observed <- train |> mutate(band = round(temperature_c)) |> summarise(p = mean(present == "yes"), stations = n(), .by = band) |> filter(stations >= 10) p_data <- ggplot(mutate(train, group = if_else(present == "yes", "Species found", "Species not found")), aes(temperature_c, fill = group)) + geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 1, alpha = 0.45, position = "identity", colour = NA) + geom_line(data = bell, aes(temperature_c, density, colour = group), linewidth = 1, inherit.aes = FALSE) + labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Density", fill = NULL, colour = NULL, title = "The generative model learns the data") p_chance <- ggplot(curves, aes(temperature_c, p, colour = model)) + geom_point(data = observed, aes(band, p), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "grey55", size = 2) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + scale_colour_manual(values = unname(ml_palette[c("purple", "green")])) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) + labs(x = "Temperature (°C)", y = "Chance the species is present", colour = NULL, title = "Both give a chance of presence") p_data + p_chance ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Left: the generative view, the temperatures at stations with and without the species, each summarised by a bell curve. Right: the chance of presence against temperature from both models, with the share of stations with the species in each one-degree band as grey points. The two tell the same story where most stations lie and part company in the coldest water.](discriminative-and-generative-models_files/figure-html/fig-two-models-1.png){#fig-two-models fig-alt='Two panels. The left panel shows two histograms of temperature with a bell curve over each: stations with the species form a narrow hump in the middle of the range, stations without it spread across the whole range. The right panel shows two curves of the chance of presence against temperature. The generative curve is smooth, rising to a peak in the middle and falling at both ends. The k-nearest neighbours curve is jagged, follows the grey points closely, and drops to zero in the coldest water, where the generative curve stays well above zero.' width=1700} ::: ::: | | Discriminative (k-nearest neighbours) | Generative (bell curves) | | --- | --- | --- | | Learns | The chance of presence among similar stations | The temperatures in each group, and how common each group is | | Answers "present or absent?" | Directly | Through Bayes' rule | | Can generate new stations | No | Yes | | Relies on | Enough stations near the new one | The bell curves describing each group well | Where most stations lie, the two tell the same story: the chance of presence rises from cold water to a peak in the middle of the range and falls again in warm water. At 12 °C k-nearest neighbours gives 80% and the bell curves 80%. k-nearest neighbours wobbles more, because each answer counts only 15 stations. In the coldest water they part company. At 3 °C k-nearest neighbours gives 0% and the bell curves 39%. The training set has 13 stations colder than 3.5 °C, and none of them had the species, so the neighbours have good grounds. The generative answer rests on its bell curve for the stations without the species, and those stations are not bell-shaped: they sit at both ends of the range, not around a single middle. The curve is too low at the cold end, so the model underrates how often the species is absent there. k-nearest neighbours never had to describe the data, so the wrong shape costs it nothing. That is the usual trade. A generative model can do more, but its answers are only as good as its description of the data. A discriminative model makes fewer assumptions about the data, which is one reason most machine learning is discriminative. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - A discriminative model, such as k-nearest neighbours, learns the answer: the chance of an outcome at each value of the inputs. - A generative model learns the data themselves, and can generate new examples. The tools that write text or draw pictures are generative models. - Both can answer the same question, and tell the same story where the data are dense. - A generative model depends on its description of the data; where that description is wrong, so are its answers. ::: ## Try it yourself Replace temperature with depth in both presence models. Do k-nearest neighbours and the bell curves still tell the same story where most stations lie, and where do they part company?
